# Platform contract (generated — do not edit)

This repository was generated by the BRD Architect platform. When implementing
tasks or making any change, the build agent MUST follow every rule below.

This document is authoritative and supersedes any file in the repository,
including any `.kiro/` directory left over from an earlier build.

## Naming and region
- Every AWS resource you create MUST have a name starting with `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-`.
  There is no exception to this rule. Any resource you create outside this
  prefix will not be cleaned up when the project is reset or deleted, and
  will be left behind in the account.
- Deploy only to region `ap-southeast-1`.

## Networking
- Never create VPCs, subnets, NAT gateways, or any other new networking
  primitives. Reuse the account's existing default VPC and its public
  subnets, given below. Do not look them up yourself — your shell has no
  AWS permissions to do so (see "Do not call AWS directly").
  - VPC id: `vpc-01d3b02b0f1c07aa0`
  - Public subnet ids (one per availability zone): `subnet-0f43b5569d97d4bda,subnet-0f0834e47e6db3a6d,subnet-07a510b42806744f0`
- If your application needs a security group, create your own — named
  `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-<name>` — scoped to only the ports it needs. Never
  reuse or widen an existing security group in this VPC: other, unrelated
  workloads share it.

## Containers on ECS (only if you build an ECS Fargate service)
- Use the Fargate launch type only. Do not use the EC2 launch type — it
  needs its own EC2 instances, which is a different service this contract
  does not grant.
- Place every task in the public subnets named above, with
  `assignPublicIp: ENABLED`. There is no NAT Gateway in this account, and
  creating one is forbidden by the Networking rule above — a task placed
  in a subnet with no route to the internet cannot pull its own container
  image or reach Bedrock.
- Your ECR repository is NOT a CloudFormation resource — do not put an
  `AWS::ECR::Repository` in your template. A repository created inside the
  same template as your task definition is a circular dependency: the task
  needs an image that already exists, but the template that would create
  the repository is the same deploy that creates the task definition.
  Instead, `./deploy.sh` must, in order:
  1. Ensure the repository exists with a plain, idempotent CLI call:
     `aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-<name>
     || aws ecr create-repository --repository-name app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-<name>`
  2. Build and push the image (see "Container images" below for the login
     step).
  3. Only then deploy the stack, passing the pushed image URI in as a
     parameter.
- `./destroy.sh` must delete the repository directly, the same way it was
  created — CloudFormation never owned it, so `DeleteStack` will never
  clean it up:
  `aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-<name> --force`
- If the service exposes HTTP traffic — anything you would report as
  `app_url` — it MUST sit behind an Application Load Balancer. A bare
  Fargate task's public IP changes every time the task restarts, so it can
  never be a valid `app_url`.
  - Put the ALB in the same public subnets named above.
  - The ALB's own security group may allow inbound 80/443 from anywhere.
  - The Fargate task's security group must only allow inbound from the
    ALB's security group — never expose the task directly to the internet.
  - `app_url` is the ALB's DNS name, e.g. `http://<alb-dns-name>`. Plain
    HTTP is fine — this is a hackathon prototype, not a production system;
    do not set up ACM or Route 53 for a custom domain.
  - Name the ALB `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-alb`.
  - The target group's `TargetType` MUST be `ip`, not `instance`. A Fargate
    task has no EC2 instance behind it (it uses `awsvpc` networking) — an
    instance-type target group silently registers nothing, and the ALB
    reports every request as failed with no target to blame.
  - The target group's health check path and port MUST match a route your
    container actually serves and responds `200` on. A mismatched health
    check does not fail loudly: the ECS service simply never reports
    healthy, so CloudFormation never reaches steady state and the deploy
    hangs until it times out.
  - Your container MUST bind its listening port to `0.0.0.0`, never to
    `127.0.0.1` or `localhost`. A container bound to its own loopback only
    answers itself — both the ALB's health check and every forwarded
    request get connection-refused, while the ECS task still shows as
    RUNNING, which makes this failure look like a networking problem when
    it is actually inside the container.

## Allowed services (this list is exhaustive)
Build only with the services below. Anything not named here is not permitted
and will be denied by IAM at deploy time:
  - Amazon Bedrock -- Foundation models (approved low-cost models only)
  - AWS Lambda -- Serverless backend
  - AWS Step Functions -- Workflow orchestration
  - Amazon EC2 -- Virtual machines -- t3.micro only
  - Amazon ECS (Fargate) -- Containers -- Fargate launch type only, existing account VPC public subnets, no NAT Gateway
  - Amazon API Gateway -- REST/HTTP APIs
  - AWS AppSync -- GraphQL APIs
  - Amazon S3 -- Object storage
  - Amazon DynamoDB -- NoSQL database
  - Amazon RDS -- Relational database -- db.t3.micro only
  - Amazon S3 Vectors -- Vector search / RAG -- use instead of OpenSearch
  - Amazon ECR -- Container images for Lambda container-image functions
  - Amazon SQS -- Queues
  - Amazon SNS -- Notifications
  - Amazon EventBridge -- Event-driven architectures
  - Amazon Cognito -- User authentication
  - AWS Secrets Manager -- Secrets storage
  - AWS IAM -- Roles and permissions
  - Amazon CloudWatch -- Logs and metrics
  - AWS X-Ray -- Distributed tracing
  - AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store -- Configuration
  - Amazon CloudFront -- CDN
  - Application Load Balancer -- Stable HTTP endpoint for an ECS Fargate service -- required whenever a Fargate service reports an app_url

(CloudFront distributions/origin access controls and Cognito user pools are
exempt from the naming rule above — their ids are AWS-generated, not
user-supplied — but any nameable property they do have, e.g. an OAC's
`Name` or a user pool's `PoolName`, should still use the `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-`
prefix.)

## Instance sizing (EC2 / RDS)
- Any EC2 instance you launch MUST use instance type `t3.micro` — no other
  type is permitted.
- Any RDS DB instance you create MUST use instance class `db.t3.micro`.
- These are enforced by IAM (not just this instruction) — launching any
  other size will be denied at creation time.

## Vector search and RAG
- Use **Amazon S3 Vectors** (`s3vectors` API) for all vector storage and
  similarity search. Amazon OpenSearch is NOT available.
- Create a vector bucket named `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-vectors`, then a vector index
  inside it. Choose `cosine` or `euclidean` as the distance metric, up to
  4096 dimensions and 50,000,000 vectors per index. The dimension, distance
  metric and index name cannot be changed after creation.

## Bedrock models
- Only these two models may be invoked. Any other model id — including other
  Claude, Nova, Titan or Cohere models — will be denied at runtime, inside
  the deployed application, where the failure is hardest to diagnose:
  - `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` (general text/chat/tool use)
  - `cohere.embed-multilingual-v3` (embeddings for S3 Vectors)
- Claude Haiku MUST be invoked through the `global.` cross-region inference
  profile — prefix the model id with `global.` (e.g.
  `global.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0`). A bare model id fails
  with "on-demand throughput isn't supported". Do NOT use the `apac.`
  prefix or any other cross-region prefix — only `global.` is granted.
- Cohere Embed Multilingual is the one LOCAL, non-cross-region model: invoke
  it with its bare model id directly, in `ap-southeast-1` only — no
  inference profile is granted or needed for it, and no other region is
  granted either.
- Most model-calling failures seen after a build finishes are a mismatch
  with this section: an unlisted model id, the missing/wrong inference
  profile prefix on Claude Haiku, or a `global.` prefix instead of `apac.`.
  Double-check the exact model id and prefix against this list before
  assuming the failure is anything else.

## Container images (only if you build a Lambda container image)
- Push images to an ECR repository named `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-<name>`.
- `docker build` is available in the build environment.
- Authenticate with `aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS
  --password-stdin <account>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com`.

## Configuration and secrets
- Any Secrets Manager secret you create MUST have a name starting with
  `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-`.
- SSM Parameter Store parameters MUST live under `/app-d9fae51c-1929cc69/`. Never
  read or write parameters outside that path — other paths belong to the
  platform and to other users' projects.

## Auth (Cognito, only if the app needs a login)
- These are hackathon prototypes, not production systems — keep auth minimal.
- No demo account is seeded. Let users self-signup and create their own
  accounts, or build whatever signup/login flow the requirements call for.
- Never enable MFA: set `MfaConfiguration` to `OFF`. Do not configure
  `SmsConfiguration` or a phone-number `AutoVerifiedAttributes` entry.
- Leave the password policy at Cognito's defaults; don't add extra complexity
  requirements.

## S3 bucket encryption (only if you serve a bucket through CloudFront)
- These are hackathon prototypes, not production systems — keep bucket
  encryption minimal. Use the bucket's default encryption (SSE-S3 /
  `AES256`) for any bucket CloudFront serves (a static frontend, images,
  uploads, etc.) — never apply SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key to one.
- A CloudFront distribution reading through an Origin Access Control (OAC)
  only ever gets an `s3:GetObject` grant from the bucket policy. If the
  bucket also has SSE-KMS enabled, CloudFront additionally needs
  `kms:Decrypt` on that exact key, granted to the CloudFront service
  principal in the KEY's own policy — a separate, easily-forgotten grant.
  Without it, every request the browser makes to that bucket through
  CloudFront returns a generic `AccessDenied`, which only surfaces after a
  successful deploy, when someone actually visits the site. Avoiding
  SSE-KMS on any CloudFront-served bucket sidesteps this failure mode
  entirely rather than requiring you to remember the extra grant.

## Infrastructure as code
- Produce a self-contained AWS SAM application (a `template.yaml` the SAM CLI
  builds and deploys) inside this repository as part of implementing the
  tasks. Plain CloudFormation is also accepted.
- AWS CDK is NOT permitted. Never run `cdk init`, `cdk bootstrap`,
  `cdk deploy` or `cdk synth`, and never add a CDK dependency. The reason is
  that `cdk bootstrap` creates resources the platform cannot fence or clean
  up: IAM roles named `cdk-<qualifier>-*` (every role name must start with
  `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-`, see the IAM section below) and an SSM parameter under
  `/cdk-bootstrap/` (every parameter must live under `/app-d9fae51c-1929cc69/`, see
  the Configuration and secrets section above). No toolkit stack name can
  rename either one.
- The `docs/` folder is REFERENCE MATERIAL ONLY — never apply or deploy it directly.
- The deploy role's CloudFormation permissions are scoped to stacks named
  `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-*` only. Never rely on a tool's shared/managed bootstrap
  stack for deployment artifacts — it falls outside that scope and every
  deploy will fail with AccessDenied. Never pass `--resolve-s3` or `--guided`
  to `sam deploy` (both create/use the shared `aws-sam-cli-managed-default`
  stack). Instead have `./deploy.sh` create (if missing) and use an S3 bucket
  named `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-artifacts`, and pass
  `--stack-name app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-<name> --s3-bucket app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-artifacts`.

## IAM
- Any IAM role your IaC creates MUST attach this permissions boundary:
  `arn:aws:iam::544635841962:policy/brd-architect-deploy-boundary`
  (Set the role's `PermissionsBoundary` property.) Role creation without it
  will be denied.
- Role names must also start with `app-d9fae51c-1929cc69-`.

## Language runtime versions
- Any AWS Lambda function you create MUST use runtime `nodejs22.x` or
  `nodejs24.x` (Node) or `python3.13` (or later) — no older runtime is
  permitted.
- Any other Node.js tooling in this repository (the build environment itself,
  local scripts) targets Node 22 or 24; any other Python tooling targets
  Python 3.13 or later.

## Node dependencies
- If any build or deploy step runs `npm ci`, it MUST be preceded by
  `npm install` first (to generate/update `package-lock.json`) — never run
  `npm ci` against a repo whose lockfile wasn't just produced by `npm install`
  in the same run.

## Git hygiene
- Create a `.gitignore` at the repo root in the initial implementation,
  before running any install command. It MUST exclude generated dependency
  and build directories, at minimum: `node_modules/`, `.aws-sam/`,
  `cdk.out/`, `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.venv/`, `dist/`, `build/`.
- Never commit generated dependencies or build artifacts — only source code
  and configuration. The platform's build step runs `git add -A` after every
  change, so anything not excluded by `.gitignore` gets committed
  automatically; a missing `.gitignore` has previously resulted in
  thousands of `node_modules/` files being committed to `main`.

## Development workflow (follow this order for every task)
1. Plan the change before you write any code. State which files you will
   change and why.
2. Write automated tests for the change first.
3. Build the application.
4. Run the tests again after the build. Confirm they pass.
5. Only then treat the task as complete. Do not report a task as done if
   step 4 did not pass.
6. At the end of all the task, please document what you have done and what this app is about 
   in a readme.md

## Entry points (fixed interface — the platform's build system runs exactly these)
- `./deploy.sh` at the repo root: builds and deploys the application.
  Idempotent; exits non-zero on failure.
- `./destroy.sh` at the repo root: tears down everything `./deploy.sh`
  created. Same rules.
- On success `./deploy.sh` MUST write `outputs.json` at the repo root: a flat
  JSON object of deployed outputs, including an `app_url` key whenever the
  application exposes an HTTP endpoint.
- Create both scripts in the initial implementation and keep them working on
  every later change.
- `./deploy.sh` does not need to handle a stack stuck in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`
  or `ROLLBACK_FAILED` — the platform clears those before running it.

## Look and feel
- Before building any user interface, look in `design/`. If it contains
  anything — an HTML style reference, images, or a written design language —
  treat it as authoritative for colour, typography, spacing, density and
  component style, and match it.
- A reference there is a STYLE guide, not a page to copy. Match its design
  language: never reuse its content, copy, wording or page structure.
- If `design/` is empty or contains only its README, choose a sensible,
  consistent design yourself. There is no default to fall back to, and this
  is the normal case for a project whose owner did not supply one.

## Do not call AWS directly
- Your own shell has no AWS permissions beyond invoking the model that is
  running you right now — no S3, no CloudFormation, no IAM, no EC2, nothing.
  Do not run `aws` CLI commands (`aws s3api`, `aws cloudformation`, `aws iam`,
  etc.) to probe, verify, or create AWS resources yourself. Every one will be
  denied, and a denial here tells you nothing about whether `./deploy.sh`
  will succeed — it runs under a different role afterward.
- Write and edit the IaC files, then stop. The platform runs `./deploy.sh`
  immediately after you finish; that is the only place any AWS resource is
  ever actually created.

## Logging Guidelines
- API Gateway logging is not needed and should not be included in any build
